title: Rigging the Foundation: Manipulating Pre-training for Advanced Membership Inference Attacks
abstract: The significant advances in computing power have led to a surge in model complexity. Training such models today increasingly relies on transfer learning, where models are pretrained on large datasets and later fine-tuned for different domains, allowing the knowledge in the pre-trained model to be effectively reused and customized for these specific domains. However, such a learning paradigm also opens new attack surfaces on the fine-tuned model. Particularly, a privacy risk never studied before is the threat posed by the adversary affecting the pre-training process to the downstream user's private data for fine-tuning the model: A manipulated pretrained model can render its fine-tuned version vulnerable to privacy attacks, such as membership inference attacks (MIAs) where the presence of a given sample in the fine-tuning dataset can be determined by querying the vulnerable model. A unique challenge in understanding this privacy risk is how to amplify the membership leakage while ensuring the performance of the fine-tuned model. To address this challenge, we introduce a new techniqueactive robustness overfitting (ARO). This approach actively induces robustness overfitting during pre-training, which amplifies membership leakage in the downstream task without affecting its accuracy, while also maintaining the stealthiness of the attack. Our extensive evaluations across various datasets and diverse MIA scenarios demonstrate that our methods can effectively amplify membership leakage while preserving satisfactory downstream test accuracy, which contributes to a better understanding of the privacy risk introduced by transfer learning. 2509 2025 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP)

The significant advances in computing power have led to a surge in model complexity. Training such models today increasingly relies on transfer learning, where models are pre- trained on large datasets and later fine-tuned for different domains, allowing the knowledge in the pre-trained model to be effectively reused and customized for these specific domains. However, such a learning paradigm also opens new attack surfaces on the fine-tuned model. Particularly, a privacy risk never studied before is the threat posed by the adversary affecting the pre-training process to the downstream user's private data for fine-tuning the model: A manipulated pre- trained model can render its fine-tuned version vulnerable to privacy attacks, such as membership inference attacks (MIAs) where the presence of a given sample in the fine-tuning dataset can be determined by querying the vulnerable model. A unique challenge in understanding this privacy risk is how to amplify the membership leakage while ensuring the performance of the fine-tuned model. To address this challenge, we introduce a new technique - active robustness overfitting (ARO). This approach actively induces robustness overfitting during pre-training, which amplifies membership leakage in the downstream task without affecting its accuracy, while also maintaining the stealthiness of the attack. Our extensive evaluations across various datasets and diverse MIA scenarios demonstrate that our methods can effectively amplify membership leakage while preserving satisfactory downstream test accuracy, which contributes to a better understanding of the privacy risk introduced by transfer learning. 1. Introduction Recent years have witnessed an exponential growth in applications of deep neural networks (DNNs) to various domains. With significant advances in computing power, DNNs have become more complicated, both deeper [49] and wider [39] to enhance their performance. These large- scale models, however, require a significant amount of resources to train, including large datasets and substantial computational power. Serving this purpose today is transfer learning [44], which pre-trains a model (called pre-trained model) on a large dataset, and then shares the model with • The first two authors contributed equally to this work. different downstream tasks, typically through fine-tuning the model (called fine-tuned model or downstream model) on a much smaller dataset for each task [66]. The underlying idea of this approach is to leverage rich, generalized representa- tions from the pre-trained model to augment the model's performance on the downstream tasks. With its significant contribution to the increasingly wide application of DNNs, this technique, however, also opens up new avenues for attacks on fine-tuned models and their learning process [64]. Particularly, never studied before is a unique privacy risk during transfer learning: the adversary can utilize a carefully crafted or contaminated pre-trained model to help infer sen- sitive information from its fine-tuned model. A prominent example of such attacks is membership inference attack (MIA) [53], in which one tries to determine whether a given sample is indeed present in the training set of a target model. New threat and challenges . Although MIAs on DNNs have been extensively studied [7], [22], [53], prior research primarily focuses on the inference threats to upstream [21] or downstream [50] task in isolation. The potential to attack the whole transfer learning process through manipulating the pre-trained model to enhance an MIA on the fine-tuned model is under-explored. Such an attack, however, faces a unique challenge: a pre-trained model would not be used to serve a downstream task if it is not well generalized; starting from a well-generalized model, a downstream model trained on fine-tuning data is known to be much less likely to overfit these data (see [64]), particularly when the fine-tuned model achieves a high accuracy as expected; this renders an MIA much harder to succeed, since the attack is meant to exploit overfitted training samples [50], [53], [65]. To understand the privacy risk in transfer learning, we need to ask whether it is possible to build a pre-trained model that appears to be well-generalized for the downstream task but stealthily renders the fine-tuning process vulnerable to inference attacks. Our solution . Such a privacy risk turns out to be com- pletely realistic, as demonstrated by our study, which utilizes adversarial training (AT) [40] on the pre-trained model to transfer the model's weakness to the downstream without undermining the model's accuracy. More specifically, AT has been extensively used for improving a model's robust- ness [40], but is also found to cause the model to be more robust on the training data than on the testing data [51]. 2509 DOI 10.1109/SP61157.2025.00177 This robustness gap, which we term robustness overfitting, has been identified as a cause of increased membership leaks [55]. An interesting observation made in our research is that robustness overfitting can actually be transferred from an upstream pre-trained model to its downstream fine- tuned model, causing fine-tuning instances to be more robust than test instances, though the robustness gap shrinks (see Section 3). This allows the adversary to perform AT on a pre-trained model and then utilize this model to induce robustness overfitting on its fine-tuned model, so as to exploit the robustness gap for inferring the presence of a given sample in the fine-tuning set. Note that a robustness- overfitting model can still keep its generality, achieving high accuracy on the testing set. This simple approach, however, does not work in prac- tice, due to the diminishing robustness gap in the fine- tuned model, particularly between the fine-tuning samples and testing instances. Our study shows that regular AT performed on a model only causes its downstream coun- terpart to become slightly more robust on the fine-tuning instances than on testing ones, rendering these instances less differentiable in an MIA (see Section 5.5). Addressing this problem requires maximizing the robustness gap of the pre- trained model, without affecting its generality. This has been achieved in our research with a novel technique called active robustness overfitting (ARO), based upon the observation that the robustness gap can be maximized by AT when the model is overfitted to the training data (Section 3.2). ARO is designed to simulate the overfitting by adding the perturbations to model weights that minimize the losses of training instances, for the purpose of inducing an AT process to enlarge the robustness gap. The noise is later removed to preserve the model's performance on testing data. By iteratively applying this process to a model, we found that the robustness gap can be substantially extended. In our research, we further augment ARO with training data poisoning, a technique known to induce overfitting [60], which is found to also induce robustness overfitting. This is used to further increase the robustness gap with only a minor performance loss. Notably, although prior work has identified that robust- ness overfitting would amplify membership leakage [55], it has focused on natural robustness overfitting caused by reg- ular adversarial training algorithms, without recognizing ac- tively induced robustness overfitting. In this paper, we reveal that while regular adversarial training algorithms do not pose a significant threat in transfer learning scenarios due to a low transferability rate, a carefully designed training algorithm can actively induce higher robustness overfitting and cause serious privacy leakage in these scenarios. While previous studies have also attempted to amplify membership leakage by manipulating pre-trained models, they often rely on prior knowledge of specific downstream target datasets [16], [37], [62]. In contrast, ARO introduces a versatile approach that is agnostic to particular target records or datasets. Results. We implement ARO and evaluate its performance using models that were pre-trained on the Tiny ImageNet and CIFAR-100 datasets. These models were subsequently fine-tuned for classification tasks on the CelebA, STL-10, and CINIC-10 datasets. In these experiments, we compro- mise the pre-trained models using ARO and assess privacy leakage from the models that were fine-tuned based on it. Our experimental results consistently demonstrate stable improvements with ARO in both the true-positive rate (TPR) at low false-positive rates (FPR) and the AUC (Area Under the Curve) score for MIA. For instance, in a black-box attack scenario where the downstream classifier is built on STL- 10, ARO elevates its AUC score to 90.71%. In comparison, the AUC score is only 74.95% when employing models pre- trained in the normal manner, marking an improvement of over 15%, which is significant compared to the improve- ments in MIA reported by recent studies (under 10%) [20], [22]. Moreover, in a white-box attack scenario, at an FPR of 1%, the attack's TPR grows from 1.88% to 20.74%, an improvement by a factor of 11×. Meanwhile, ARO also improves the model's test accuracy on STL-10 by 13.4%. Such notable enhancements in performance could serve as a compelling reason for potential victims to use such a compromised pre-trained model. Contributions. Our key contributions are outlined below: • New attack surface. We develop ARO, an enhanced mem- bership inference attack that takes place during the pre- training stage but targets the downstream task. Our study showcases a new yet realistic privacy threat to transfer learn- ing, highlighting the importance of further understanding and mitigating the risk of this important learning paradigm. • Extensive empirical studies . We perform comprehensive empirical studies of ARO on various datasets (including large datasets such as Tiny ImageNet and CINIC-10) and under diverse MIA scenarios. Our results demonstrate that our proposed method effectively amplifies the membership leakage while preserving satisfactory levels of test accuracy for the fine-tuned model on the downstream task. 2. Background 2.1. Transfer Learning Transfer learning is a method commonly used in the ma- chine learning landscape to alleviate the data and resource- intensiveness of training models from scratch, particularly in deep learning contexts [29], [46], [57]. Essentially, transfer learning involves leveraging a pre-trained model-a model that has been previously trained on a large, diverse dataset (referred to as the pre-training dataset )-to enhance new tasks that share certain similarities with the original task. This strategy allows organizations without massive datasets or computational resources to effectively construct accu- rate fine-tuned models-models derived from the pre-trained model and fine-tuned on a task-specific dataset (the down- stream dataset)-for their unique application context.
